# Introduction

Imaging surveys publish a catalogue of every source they detect, and those
catalogues hold galaxies that no galaxy catalogue lists. Recovering them need
not start from the pixels. @tanoglidis2021cat selected low-surface-brightness
candidates from the Dark Energy Survey source catalogue, classified them by
machine and inspected the survivors by eye, while SMUDGes [@zaritsky2019] runs
its own detection on the imaging. Both checked every object they kept by eye,
as did @thuruthipilly2024. At $10^5$ entries one inspector cannot, so purity
has to be measured on a sample and doubtful entries flagged. We start from the
source catalogue of the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys [@dey2019], measured with
Tractor [@lang2016]. Cuts on those measurements and a screen against existing
identifications select the catalogue, an inspected sample measures its purity,
and two classifiers flag doubtful entries.

Low-surface-brightness (LSB) galaxies are under-represented in every major
galaxy catalogue, because of the selection functions of the surveys those
catalogues come from [@zaritsky2019], and our selection window lies at
low surface brightness for that reason. @tanoglidis2021 trained convolutional
networks ("DeepShadows") to separate LSB galaxies from imaging artefacts in
the Dark Energy Survey, and their visually labelled sample is now a benchmark.

Convolutional networks are designed for problems whose useful features have
to be learned. For a galaxy the useful features are known in advance, because its
light is close to elliptically symmetric, and its departures from that symmetry, such as bars, arms and lopsidedness, are features in their own right. Binning the light in
concentric annuli puts the symmetry into the representation directly, so no
network has to learn it. We test whether that representation, with a standard
classifier, matches the pixel-based deep model. We compare several classifiers
as a candidate set, in the manner of multi-model inference in ecology
[@burnham2002], reporting every member and testing whether a combination
predicts better than the best one.

The catalogue is DEBBIE (DR10 Ensemble of Boosted trees and Bidirectional
recurrent networks for Identifying Extragalactic sources), named for the two
classifiers that flag its doubtful entries (@sec-screen). No classifier decides which
candidates enter: the cuts and the screening for prior identification define
the catalogue, and the two classifiers flag likely contaminants without
removing any. It holds
{{N_COMMA}} galaxy candidates in DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys DR10
with no prior identification as galaxies in the catalogues and services we
queried. We measure its selection function on real catalogued galaxies in
place of synthetic injections (@sec-selfn), and the whole selection can be
recomputed from a released 3.2 GB source extract.

[Fig. @fig-pipeline] shows the steps and the count that leaves each one.
@sec-data describes the survey and benchmark data and @sec-radial the radial
representation. @sec-classification tests the representation on the benchmark,
@sec-catalogue presents the catalogue with its selection function and purity,
@sec-compare compares it with the DES and SMUDGes catalogues, and @sec-summary
lists the results.

# Data {#sec-data}

## Survey data

We use the DR10 south *sweep* catalogues, which hold the survey's Tractor
photometry: positions, morphological types, shape parameters, and forced
photometry in $g$, $r$, $z$ and the WISE bands. Every candidate is a source
Tractor detected and measured, so the catalogue inherits Tractor's
completeness, which @sec-selfn measures.

The main catalogue covers DR10 south at Galactic latitude $|b| \ge 30^\circ$.
We processed all 874 sweep files in that region, an occupied area of about
{{AREA_COMMA}} deg$^2$. We stop at $|b| = 30^\circ$ because at lower latitude
Galactic cirrus looks like diffuse galaxies and foreground extinction corrupts
the surface-brightness selection. The sweeps at $12^\circ < |b| < 30^\circ$
yield {{N_EXT_COMMA}} further candidates, released as a separately flagged
extension that carries a cirrus-contamination caveat and enters none of the
statistics reported here.

## Benchmark data

For classifier comparisons we use the DeepShadows sample [@tanoglidis2021],
restricted to their objects and to their visually confirmed hard-negative
class (`artifact_hard_visually_rejected`), the class their published AUC is
measured on. Including the easier negatives, which an earlier
support-vector-machine stage of their pipeline rejected, raises the AUC
of every method by about 0.014, so we leave them out and the comparison with
the published AUC stays like for like.

The published model was trained on 30,000 objects and ours on the {{BM_NTRAIN}}
available to us. It also works on different pixels, because the CNN works on DES
imagery with DES photometry while we measure the same sky positions in DR10
imaging with our own measurements. The two pipelines therefore share only their
labels, and any gap between them mixes the classifier with the imaging and the
training size.
@sec-ablation makes the controlled comparison, with everything but the
features held fixed.

# Radial representation {#sec-radial}

We measure each source in 24 concentric annuli with radii spaced
geometrically from 1 to 84$''$, each divided into 32 position-angle cells, in
each of $g$, $r$ and $z$ ([Fig. @fig-representation]). For each annulus we keep the mean and the median over position angle and the
amplitudes of the first four azimuthal Fourier modes, from a discrete Fourier
transform over the cells. Low-order Fourier terms have long been used in
isophote analysis [@jedrzejewski1987; @rix1995], and they encode lopsidedness
and ellipticity without a shape fit. We keep the median as well as the mean
because the median is robust to one bright neighbour in a single wedge.

We track the coverage of each cell against the count it would have if the
frame were complete, so clipping at a brick edge registers as reduced coverage
and does not look like a faint annulus. Each profile is extracted twice, at
the catalogue position and at a flux-weighted refined centroid. We keep both,
and the offset between the two centres is itself a feature, because a large
offset flags blends and fragments. The feature definitions are in the
released code.

(a) DEBBIE 37011, accepted as a galaxy in the inspection of @sec-purity, with a

pixel. Colour images: Legacy Surveys / D. Lang (Perimeter

# Classification results {#sec-classification}

## Benchmark

On a balanced test set of {{BM_NTEST}} objects ({{BM_NPER}} per class), split by object and
evaluated once, gradient-boosted trees [@chen2016] on the radial
representation reach AUC {{BM_AUC}}, with a 2,000-resample bootstrap interval of
[{{BM_LO}}, {{BM_HI}}]. The published CNN reports 0.9740 (published range
0.9700--0.9740) on the same object and negative classes. The same classifier
on six conventional catalogue features (profile monotonicity,
concentration, signal-to-noise ratio, angular radius, central surface
brightness and local imaging depth) reaches {{BM_SIX}} [{{BM_SIX_LO}}, {{BM_SIX_HI}}]
([Fig. @fig-benchmark]). The classifiers are XGBoost 3.4.0 and scikit-learn
1.9.0. The trees use one setting throughout (400 trees of depth 4, learning
rate 0.06, row and column subsampling 0.85), fixed before the benchmark was
run, and the released code fixes the splits and seeds.

![On the DeepShadows benchmark, the radial representation raises the AUC of
one gradient-boosted classifier from {{BM_SIX}} to {{BM_AUC}}, above the
published CNN. Filled points: the same classifier on two inputs, on the same
test split, with 2,000-resample bootstrap intervals. Open point: the published
CNN with its published range; it was trained on more objects and on DES images
(@sec-data).](figures/fig2_benchmark){#fig-benchmark}

## Representation versus architecture {#sec-ablation}

We separate the representation from the model with a controlled ablation: one
gradient-boosted classifier and four feature sets, so that only the
classifier's input varies. The first test split is held out by sky position,
so each field falls on one side of it; we call it the frozen spatial fold. On
that fold, six conventional catalogue features score {{FZ_SIX}}, the per-annulus
profile alone (144 features) {{FZ_PROF}}, that profile plus the six catalogue
features (150) {{FZ_P6}}, and the full flattened representation (1,023) {{FZ_FULL}}.

On five other test splits the same
six-feature model scored between 0.861 and 0.911, so the choice of split alone
moves an absolute AUC by about 0.05, nearly as much as the improvement from the six
catalogue features to the full representation. We therefore
repeated all four feature sets over five stratified folds of the benchmark
sample ({{MM_NPOS}} galaxies and {{MM_NNEG}} hard negatives) and scored each on
every fold (@tbl-ablation). The ordering is the same on all five. The paired
improvement from six catalogue features to the full representation is
${{MM_GAIN}} \pm {{MM_GAIN_SD}}$ and is at least ${{MM_GAIN_MIN}}$ on every
fold. Pairing matters because the difficulty of a split is common to all four
and cancels in the difference, so the uncertainty that applies is the
{{MM_GAIN_SD}} spread of the paired improvement.

| model | features | mean AUC | sd |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| trees, six catalogue features | 6 | {{MM_SIX}} | {{MM_SIX_SD}} |
| trees, per-annulus profile | 144 | {{MM_PROF}} | {{MM_PROF_SD}} |
| trees, profile + six catalogue features | 150 | {{MM_P6}} | {{MM_P6_SD}} |
| trees, full flattened representation | 1,023 | {{MM_FULL}} | {{MM_FULL_SD}} |
| recurrent network on the annuli | sequence | {{MM_GRU}} | {{MM_GRU_SD}} |
| mean of the last two | | {{MM_DUAL}} | {{MM_DUAL_SD}} |

: The candidate models over five stratified folds of the benchmark sample,
with identical folds throughout. In the first four rows only the input to the
trees changes, and the representation raises the AUC by ${{MM_GAIN}}$; the
recurrent network on the annuli alone matches the trees, and the mean of the
two is the score that flags catalogue entries. {#tbl-ablation}

These five folds are randomly stratified, with fields shared between training
and test, so their absolute values are optimistic next to the frozen spatial fold, as the
two sets of numbers show. We therefore claim only the paired comparisons. The
ablation shows that the representation carries information the six catalogue
features lack.

The same folds compare architectures and test whether combining the
candidates predicts better than the best one alone. A bidirectional recurrent network that
takes the annuli in order of radius, without the six catalogue features,
scores {{MM_GRU}}. That is level with the trees on the full representation, with
a paired difference of ${{MM_GRU_D}} \pm {{MM_GRU_D_SD}}$ that favours the
network on {{MM_GRU_POS}} folds of five.

Ecologists weight each member of a candidate set by its support and predict from the weighted set
[@burnham2002]. Astronomy uses information criteria and model averaging to choose
between cosmological models [@liddle2007; @parkinson2013], and classifier
ensembles are common in source classification [@kim2015], including on these
labels [@thuruthipilly2024]. Trees have no parameter count, so in place of the
Akaike information criterion we weighted each model by its deviance on held-out
parts of the training fold. With about {{MM_NTRAIN}} training objects per fold one model
takes more than 0.99 of the weight on every fold, so weighting reduces to
selection. An unweighted mean of the trees and the recurrent
network scores {{MM_DUAL}}, which is ${{MM_DUAL_D}} \pm {{MM_DUAL_D_SD}}$
above the trees and higher on all five folds, with a log-loss {{MM_DUAL_LL}}%
lower. A mean over all five candidates is {{MM_ALL_D}} below the trees,
because the weaker members lower it. Combining improves the AUC about
{{MM_RATIO}} times less than the representation does.

# Catalogue {#sec-catalogue}

## Selection {#sec-selection}

From the sweep catalogues we select sources that meet all of the following: a
resolved morphological type (`EXP`, `DEV`, `SER` or `REX`; Tractor assigns
`SHAPE_R` = 0 to PSF sources, so this excludes point sources exactly);
$r_{\rm eff} \ge 3''$; mean surface brightness within the effective radius,
$\mu_{\rm eff}$, between 24.0 and 26.5 mag arcsec$^{-2}$ in $g$; at least two
exposures in both $g$ and $r$; a $z$-band detection; and `MASKBITS` = 0. The
$z$-band requirement is the weaker, single-epoch one because $z$-band epoch
counts are lower over parts of the southern footprint. The faint edge of the
surface-brightness window matters most. Above $\mu_{\rm eff} = 26.5$ Tractor
increasingly fits large radii to noise, and in 48-object contact sheets of an
early pool, 62% of which lay above that threshold, such sources mostly looked
like background fluctuations.

## Novelty screening {#sec-novelty}

We reject any candidate within 20$''$ of one of the 138,675,216 catalogued
objects in a local index: the full HyperLEDA catalogue [@makarov2014], SDSS DR12
photometric galaxies to $r = 22.5$ between right ascensions 120$^\circ$ and
235$^\circ$ [@alam2015], GLADE+ [@dalya2022], the 2MASS Extended Source
Catalog [@jarrett2000], 2dFGRS [@colless2001], 6dFGS [@jones2009], SMUDGes
[@zaritsky2019], and 28.5 million DES DR2 sources over part of the southern
footprint [@abbott2021des]. The local screen runs at $4.5\times10^{5}$
positions s$^{-1}$, fast enough to screen every candidate. We then query each
survivor against NED within 30$''$, counting any object of a galaxy type as an
identification, against SMUDGes within 15$''$, and against SIMBAD within
15$''$, where any object at all counts against the candidate. A query that
fails is repeated, and a failed check is never recorded as novelty. The
queries ran in order of decreasing $r_{\rm eff}$ and did not reach
{{SA_NEVER}} candidates, {{SA_NEVER_SMALL}} of them below 3.05$''$, just above
the size limit. These are excluded, so the screen can lose a real candidate but
cannot create a spurious one.

Tractor splits extended sources into several fragments, so an outer fragment
can sit more than
20$''$ from the catalogued position of its galaxy and pass that screen. We
remove such fragments by rejecting any candidate with an object of the local
index between 20$''$ and 45$''$. The filter also discards genuine candidates.
At 20,000 random footprint positions, 22.2% have an index entry in that
annulus, and among candidates that no catalogue lists within 20$''$ the filter
removes {{FC_FRAG_PCT}}% (@sec-verifcomp). The selection function of @sec-selfn measures the
photometric cuts alone and so leaves that loss out. When Tractor splits one galaxy into
several rows that all survive, we merge them with a matching radius of
$\max(6'', r_{\rm eff})$ and keep the largest member; 2,013 entries were
merged.

A further filter removes spurious detections that cluster on defective imaging
bricks, by rejecting any candidate with three or more other candidates within
1.5$'$. We exclude one region of 6$'$ radius at
$(\alpha, \delta) = (144.79^\circ, -2.79^\circ)$ permanently, having
confirmed it by eye.

## What counts as an identification

No object in DEBBIE has a prior identification as an extragalactic object:
none passes within the radii above of a catalogued galaxy, of a NED object
typed G, GPair, GTrpl, GGroup, GClstr, QSO or AGN, or of any SIMBAD
[@wenger2000] object. A designation from an automated survey is not an
identification.
Nearly all entries ({{DESIG_PCT}}%) carry one, most often from WISE
[@wright2010], so they were detected before but never typed, and we record
every designation NED lists within 0.5$'$ of each position.

DESI DR1 [@desidr1] is a public spectroscopic release that covers this imaging
footprint and selects its targets from the same parent photometry. Matching
the candidate list against it at 2$''$ finds a reliable spectrum (ZWARN = 0)
for {{DESI_MAIN}} main-catalogue entries, {{DESI_MAIN_PCT}}% of the list, of
which {{DESI_GAL}} are typed GALAXY, {{DESI_QSO}} QSO and {{DESI_STAR}} STAR.
The galaxies and quasars have a published spectroscopic identification as
extragalactic, which our definition counts as prior identification, and the
stars are not galaxies. We remove all {{DESI_MAIN}}, which
leaves {{N12}} entries, and every number in this paper is computed on that
set.

Of the {{DESI_REL}} main-set entries with a reliable DESI classification,
{{DESI_PURITY}}% are extragalactic and {{DESI_STAR}} are stars. That figure
overstates the purity of the catalogue. Every matched row is a deliberate DESI
target, and DESI chose its targets from this same Legacy photometry with cuts
(BGS, LRG, ELG) that are themselves galaxy selections. The match therefore
measures how often DESI's own galaxy selection picks galaxies, a number its
cuts largely decide. Those
{{DESI_REL}} objects are also the ones removed from the catalogue as already
identified, so the figure describes entries that have left it. We measure the
purity of the {{N_REMAIN}} that remain separately, by visual inspection
(@sec-purity).

Of our entries, {{PS_COV}}% appear in VII/292 [@duncan2022], the published
Legacy Surveys photometric-redshift catalogue from which we draw
{{N_LSP_COMMA}} of our redshifts, and it assigns $p_{\rm star} < 0.5$ to
{{VII292_NONSTELLAR}}% of them. A published catalogue has therefore already
treated most of these sources as non-stellar. We do not count that as
identification either, because VII/292 assigns a photometric redshift and a
star probability to every source in the parent imaging, stars and artefacts
included, and NED and SIMBAD ingest none of its entries as extragalactic
classifications. DEBBIE likewise classifies sources that Tractor had already
detected and adds no detections of its own.

VST ATLAS DR4 [@shanks2025] classes {{VST_GAL}}% of the DEBBIE entries it
detects as galaxies (@sec-purity), but it was not searched. The screen counts
automated galaxy classes only from the catalogues it searched, such as the
SDSS DR12 photometric types and GLADE+, so the novelty claim holds for the
catalogues and services above, and a wider search would find an automated
class for most entries.

The screening depends most on NED, which aggregates the identifications of
most published extragalactic surveys, and we searched no catalogue outside
these services. SMUDGes [@zaritsky2019] has already designated about
7,000 candidates found in this same imaging.

## Physical properties

Redshifts are available for {{Z_COV}}% of the catalogue, and all are
photometric, because the only spectroscopic redshifts in the candidate list
were DESI's and they left with the DESI-identified entries. Every
distance-dependent quantity below therefore depends on photometric redshifts. Of these, {{N_LSP_COMMA}} come from the Legacy Surveys DR8
photometric-redshift catalogue [VizieR VII/292, @duncan2022], matched through
the CDS X-Match service [@boch2012], and {{N_OWN_COMMA}} from a
gradient-boosted photometric-redshift model, fitted with scikit-learn
[@pedregosa2011], that we trained on our own $g r z W1$ photometry for sky outside the public photo-$z$ coverage. Against
the Legacy photo-$z$ on spatially held-out sky this estimator has
$\sigma_{\rm NMAD} = 0.046$, and a shuffled-label control degrades to 0.194.
We record the photo-$z$ source per object and keep the two estimates apart
in any analysis that depends on redshift quality.

Distances assume flat $\Lambda$CDM with $H_0 = 70$ km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$ and
$\Omega_m = 0.3$, and absolute magnitudes are not k-corrected. Stellar masses
apply the $g{-}r$ mass-to-light relation of @bell2003 to observed colours,
which is sound only at low redshift. Below $z = 0.2$ they are factor-of-two
estimates. At $z \ge 0.35$ the observed colour is far redder than the
rest-frame one, so the masses come out too high, {{MASS_HI_PCT}}% of them
above $10^{12} M_\odot$, and they should not be used there.

The median catalogue object lies at $z = {{Z_MED3}}$ with
$r_{\rm eff} = {{R_KPC}}$ kpc and $M_g = {{MG_MED}}$
([Fig. @fig-properties]), which are the parameters of an ordinary galaxy.
Cosmological surface-brightness dimming explains why such galaxies pass a
low-surface-brightness cut. The bolometric Tolman factor,
$10\log_{10}(1+z)$, is {{TOLMAN}} mag arcsec$^{-2}$ at the median redshift.
For surface brightness per unit frequency, which is what AB magnitudes
measure, the factor before any k-correction is $7.5\log_{10}(1+z)$, or
{{TOLMAN3}} mag arcsec$^{-2}$. Either is a
large part of the 2.5-mag selection window, so a normal galaxy at the median
redshift enters the window without being diffuse. The argument holds for the
population and should not be applied to a single object.

DEBBIE therefore lists previously uncatalogued galaxy candidates, most of
them distant and dimmed. The exception is a nearby tail of
{{N_DWARF_COMMA}} objects at $z < 0.05$, with median
$r_{\rm eff} = {{DWARF_RKPC}}$ kpc and median
$\log(M_\star/M_\odot) = {{DWARF_LOGM}}$, the sizes and masses of dwarfs. Of
these, {{N_UDG_COMMA}} satisfy $r_{\rm eff} > 1.5$ kpc and mean
$\mu_{\rm eff} > 24$ mag arcsec$^{-2}$, which approximates the ultra-diffuse
criteria of @vandokkum2015; those criteria are conventionally stated in
central surface brightness, and ours is the mean.

![What the catalogue contains: mostly ordinary galaxies dimmed by distance,
with median photometric redshift {{Z_MED}}. The released quantities for the
{{N_COMMA}} entries: (a) effective radius and mean $g$ surface brightness,
where the vertical stripe is {{N_PILE}} entries with $r_{\rm eff}$ of exactly
13.624$''$ (52 pixels); (b) observed colours; (c) photometric redshifts by
source; (d) physical size and stellar mass for entries at $z < 0.2$, where the
mass estimate holds.](figures/fig5_properties){#fig-properties}

## Selection function {#sec-selfn}

We measure the selection function on real catalogued galaxies in place of
synthetic injections. For each known galaxy inside the observed footprint we
ask whether the sweeps contain a resolved counterpart and whether the
photometric cuts retain it, so real profiles, neighbours and imaging defects
enter at their true rates. The measurement covers the cuts only. It excludes
the novelty screen and the fragment and clump filters, whose losses
@sec-verifcomp measures.

The reference population is the non-stellar entries of the 110-million-object
screening index, restricted to $|b| \ge 30^\circ$ and to sky the extract
covers, and matched at 3$''$. Of 235,715 such galaxies, 33,595 (14.2%) appear
in the source extract as resolved sources with $r_{\rm eff} \ge 2''$. Most of
those lie outside the surface-brightness window this catalogue targets, and
across all of them the cuts retain 10.4%. In 15 of the 17 cells
of the size and surface-brightness grid inside the selection window that hold
at least 30 reference galaxies, the photometric cuts alone retain
between 70% and 89% of them ([Fig. @fig-sky]b). The other two cells retain
56% (8--10$''$, $\mu$ 24--25) and 63% (10--15$''$, $\mu$ 24--25). Wilson 95%
intervals are 0.1--9 percentage points (half-width) for cells with at least 50
galaxies and are given cell by cell in `selection_function.json` in the
release.

Above $r_{\rm eff} = 15''$ one of 34 known galaxies survives. With $N = 34$
the Wilson 95% interval runs from 0.5% to 14.9% around a point estimate of
2.9%, so this
bounds the retention without measuring it. The cause is that Tractor splits
the largest galaxies into fragments, none of which carries the size and
surface brightness of the whole galaxy, so the cuts reject them. DEBBIE
is substantially incomplete above $r_{\rm eff} \approx 15''$ and cannot
constrain the abundance of large LSB systems.

### Losses in the screen {#sec-verifcomp}

The selection function above is not end to end. The screen removed most
candidates while the sweeps were mined, before any candidate list existed, and
recorded nothing about them, so we counted every step again by applying the
cuts to the source extract ([Fig. @fig-pipeline] gives each count). Of the
{{FC_TOTAL}} sources that pass the cuts at $|b| \ge 30^\circ$, {{FC_ID20_PCT}}%
({{FC_ID20}}) lie within 20$''$ of an object in the local index, and in
{{FC_SDSS5}} of those matches the object is an SDSS galaxy within 5$''$: SDSS had
already catalogued the candidate itself. The fragment filter removes
{{FC_FRAG}} and the clump filter {{SA_CLUMP}}. Rules used early in the mining
removed {{FC_MINED_OTHER}} more: {{FC_OLD90}} by a fragment radius of 90$''$,
since reduced to 45$''$, and {{FC_UNREC}} that left no record. The queries
never reached {{SA_NEVER}}. That leaves {{SA_QUERIED}} candidates queried, of
which NED, SIMBAD or HyperLEDA identify {{SA_KNOWN}}, and merging at export
leaves {{FC_BEFORE_DESI}} before the DESI step.

The fragment filter is the loss that matters for completeness: besides the
fragments it is meant for, it removes a genuine candidate whenever an unrelated catalogued object lies
20--45$''$ away. Among candidates that no catalogue lists within 20$''$ it
removes {{FC_FRAG_PCT}}%, almost independent of size: {{FC_FR34}}% at
$r_{\rm eff} = 3$--4$''$ and {{FC_FR1015}}% at 10--15$''$. End to end, the
selection fraction is roughly the cut retention times the share the filter
keeps: near 10--15$''$ and $\mu_{\rm eff}$ 24--25,
$0.63 \times {{FC_FR1015_KEEP}} \approx {{FC_E2E}}$. The incompleteness above
$r_{\rm eff} \approx 15''$ comes from Tractor's fragmentation of large galaxies
and says little about the sky. We release the {{UNVER_BIG}} candidates with
$r_{\rm eff} \ge 6''$ that the local screen removed from the candidate list,
with the extract, so the removals can be checked.

The selection function is completeness relative to *known* galaxies, so a
population absent from both the published catalogues and the sweeps
cannot appear in it. It also cannot be split into detection and selection terms,
because the archived source extract keeps only sources with
$r_{\rm eff} \ge 2''$, and we did not keep the raw sweeps that would allow
the split.

The catalogue is also non-uniform on the sky ([Fig. @fig-sky]a), and nearly
empty inside the SDSS imaging footprint. Between right ascensions 150$^\circ$
and 200$^\circ$ it holds {{SH_SOUTH}} entries per deg$^2$ at
$-10^\circ < \delta < -4^\circ$, south of the footprint, and {{SH_NORTH}} at
$+4^\circ < \delta < +20^\circ$, inside it. SDSS DR12 lists about
{{SH_SDSS}} photometric galaxies per deg$^2$ to $r = 22.5$ there, so a random position has on
average {{SH_N20}} within the 20$''$ screening radius and {{SH_N45}} in the
20--45$''$ fragment annulus. Most candidates there were catalogued before:
{{SA_SDSS_OWN_PCT}}% of those inside the footprint have an SDSS galaxy within
5$''$, the candidate itself, and the fragment filter removes nearly all of the
rest. DEBBIE therefore says almost nothing about that sky. Density also falls by a factor of two to four in the band
$-2^\circ < \delta < +2^\circ$ ({{DEC_B1}} and {{DEC_B2}} objects in the two
equatorial 2$^\circ$ bins, against {{DEC_NBR_LO}}--{{DEC_NBR_HI}} in the six
neighbouring bins), where prior cataloguing is densest (the SDSS equatorial
stripes, including Stripe 82). Clustering analyses must model both.

![Where the catalogue is, and how much of the known galaxy population its cuts
keep. (a) Entries per square degree in equal-area cells, right ascension
increasing to the left; solid line, the Galactic plane; dotted lines,
$|b| = 30^\circ$. North of the equator between 8h and 16h the catalogue is
nearly empty, because SDSS had already catalogued most candidates there. (b) The percentage of known galaxies present in the
sweeps that the photometric cuts keep, by size and surface brightness: 56--89%
from 3 to 15$''$, and 1 of 34 above 15$''$. Hatched cells hold fewer than 30
reference galaxies, starred cells fewer than 50.](figures/fig3_sky_selection){#fig-sky}

## Purity {#sec-purity}

![What the entries look like, at the scale of the first inspection: 75$''$
per panel at 0.375$''$ per pixel, each labelled with its designation and
effective radius. Upper block: the eight largest entries that clear every
screen. Lower block: eight drawn at random. The random draw is smaller,
fainter and more marginal, and it is what the catalogue typically contains.
Saturated stars and fields with a missing band appear as the survey images
show them. Images: Legacy Surveys / D. Lang (Perimeter
Institute).](figures/fig4_montage){#fig-montage}

Visual inspection of a stratified sample finds a galaxy at the catalogued
position for {{PF_A}}% of entries (95% CI {{PF_A_LO}}--{{PF_A_HI}}%). That
is {{PF_AB}}% ({{PF_AB_LO}}--{{PF_AB_HI}}%) for the {{PUR_B_N}} entries
with $\mu_{\rm eff} < {{PUR_SPLIT}}$ mag arcsec$^{-2}$ and {{PF_AF}}%
({{PF_AF_LO}}--{{PF_AF_HI}}%) for the {{PUR_F_N}} fainter ones.

We drew a sample of {{PURITY_N_COMMA}} objects stratified over
{{PURITY_CELLS}} cells of the ($r_{\rm eff}$, $\mu_{\rm eff}$) plane, with an
effective size of {{PURITY_NEFF_COMMA}}, the number of equally weighted objects
that would give the same precision. Each object carries the number of
catalogue entries it stands for, so every figure here is a weighted
reconstruction of the catalogue. The sample was put in random order after it
was drawn, and we inspected its first {{PUR_JUDGED}} objects, a random
subsample covering every cell, in two stages. In the first, on 75$''$ colour
cutouts at 0.375$''$ per pixel (the scale of [Fig. @fig-montage]), we accepted
{{PF_NACC}} objects as galaxies and set {{PF_NSET}} aside for closer
inspection. Each object set aside was then examined in a 30$''$ view at
0.15$''$ per pixel beside the Tractor model and the residual, and judged
galaxy, non-galaxy or undecided.

The closer inspection found a galaxy in {{PF_SET_GAL}} of the {{PF_NSET}}
objects set aside and none in {{PF_SET_NO}}, and left {{PF_SET_AMB}}
undecided. Re-examining only the objects set aside could only raise the
purity, because an accepted object that is not a galaxy would never be caught,
so {{PF_NCTL}} accepted objects went through the closer inspection as well, in
the same sitting, interleaved with the rest and unlabelled. Of the
{{PF_CTL_DEC}} that got a decision, {{PF_CTL_NO}} were rejected. We apply that
rate, within each surface-brightness half, to the accepted objects that were
not inspected again. Intervals come from a bootstrap over the sample objects,
with the rate estimated afresh in each resample.

Altogether {{PF_STILL}} objects remain undecided, the {{PF_SET_AMB}} above and
one of the re-examined accepted objects, and are left out of these
percentages;
counting every one of them as a non-galaxy gives {{PF_A_BLO}}%, and as a galaxy
{{PF_A_BHI}}%. A single inspector made every verdict, so the intervals carry
no term for disagreement between inspectors. The inspection recorded only
whether a galaxy was present, so the rejected objects are an unsorted mix of
stars, artefacts, noise and fragments of larger sources.

VST ATLAS DR4 images part of this footprint with
a different telescope, pipeline and seeing, to a point-source limit of
$r = 22.7$, and catalogues everything it detects, stars and noise included.
Matching {{VST_N}} random catalogue positions at 2$''$ finds a counterpart
for {{VST_MATCH}}%, and of those {{VST_GAL}}% carry `MERGEDCLASS` galaxy or
probable galaxy, {{VST_STAR}}% star or probable star, and {{VST_NOISE}}%
noise. That {{VST_GAL}}% is far above the inspected purity, and the inspected
sample shows why. Inside the VST footprint the inspection found {{VF_NOT_N}}
objects that are not galaxies; VST detects {{VF_NOT_M}} of them and classes
{{VF_NOT_GAL}} of those as galaxies. At these magnitudes VST calls
nearly everything it detects a galaxy.

### Stars {#sec-stars}

Stars can be identified from the catalogue's own photometry, and the released
tables flag them and keep them. We trained a gradient-boosted classifier
(XGBoost) on {{STAR_NFEAT}} Tractor quantities: the effective radius, its
inverse variance and its signal-to-noise; the signal-to-noise of the $g$ and
$r$ fluxes; the difference and ratio in $\chi^2$ between the Sérsic and
point-source fits; the Sérsic index; the two ellipticity components and their
modulus; the fraction of flux from neighbours in $g$ and $r$; the fractions
inside masks and inside the fit in $g$; Galactic reddening; the numbers of $g$
and $r$ exposures; and the $g-r$, $r-z$ and $r-W1$ colours.
The training set is the entries DESI DR1 observed, {{STAR_NGAL}} with a galaxy
spectrum at $z \ge 0.005$ against {{STAR_NSTAR}} with a stellar one. All of
them passed the catalogue's selection, and none is in the catalogue, because
the DESI-identified entries were removed. Out of fold the classifier reaches
AUC {{STAR_AUC}}, against {{STAR_AUC_P}} for the Legacy Surveys star
probability $p_{\rm star}$ [@duncan2022]. At the threshold that flags
{{STAR_GLOSS}}% of the spectroscopic galaxies it flags {{STAR_D_CLF}}% of the
spectroscopic stars.

DESI chose which stars to observe, so we tested the classifier on stars it had
not been trained on. Gaia DR3 [@gaia2016; @gaia2023], which we use nowhere else
in this work, has a source within 2$''$ of {{GAIA_MATCH}}% of {{GAIA_N}} random
catalogue positions, and {{GAIA_CERT}}% (95% CI
{{GAIA_CERT_LO}}--{{GAIA_CERT_HI}}%) show a 5$\sigma$ parallax or proper
motion and so are stars. That is a lower bound on the stellar fraction,
since Gaia astrometry reaches only the brighter entries. At the same threshold
the classifier flags {{STAR_G_CLF}}% of those {{GAIA_NCERT}} entries, against
{{STAR_D_CLF}}% of the DESI stars it was trained on.

For these sources $p_{\rm star}$ is not a calibrated probability. Its mean
over the spectroscopic galaxies is {{PS_GAL}}, against {{PS_CAT}} over the
{{PS_COV}}% of catalogue entries that have one. Summing it over the catalogue
to count stars therefore overstates them, because galaxies alone would supply
{{PS_SHARE}}% of that sum. A value above {{PS_CUT}} is still informative, since
only {{PS09_GAL}}% of the spectroscopic galaxies reach it, and we use it as a second, weaker flag for entries the classifier
passes. Together the two flag {{STAR_D_ANY}}% of the DESI stars,
{{STAR_G_ANY}}% of the Gaia stars and {{STAR_GLOSS_ANY}}% of the spectroscopic
galaxies.

Each entry carries the classifier's star score and a flag: 1 for the
{{FLAG1}} entries above the classifier threshold, and 2 for the {{FLAG2}} further entries with
$p_{\rm star} > {{PS_CUT}}$. Together they mark {{FLAG_PCT}}% of the
catalogue. Large galaxies are flagged more often than small ones,
{{STAR_GL_BIG}}% of the spectroscopic galaxies with $r_{\rm eff} \ge 6''$
against {{STAR_GL_SMALL}}% of those with $r_{\rm eff} < 4''$. Discarding
flagged entries would therefore remove large galaxies preferentially, so the
selection function of @sec-selfn describes the catalogue with them kept.

Stars are a small part of the contamination, and on the inspected sample the
flag does not separate galaxies from the rest. It marks {{PF_SL_NO_FLAG}} of the
{{PF_SL_NO}} objects the closer inspection rejected and {{SV_SF_GAL}} of the
{{SV_NGAL}} galaxies. Leaving flagged entries out moves the purity by
{{PF_STAR_DELTA}} percentage points.

### Two-model flag {#sec-screen}

The classifiers of @sec-classification were trained on profiles measured
before the Legacy Surveys cutout service changed its handling of small
cutouts, and the catalogue was measured after. We therefore re-extracted all
{{RX_N}} labelled objects behind the benchmark, of every class, through the
path the catalogue uses. The single-split AUC is
{{RX_S_NEW}}, against {{RX_S_AUG}} before, and the five-fold AUC of the trees
on the full representation is {{RX_F_NEW}}, against {{RX_F_AUG}}.

On the re-extracted benchmark we fitted the two models that flag catalogue
entries: gradient-boosted trees on the radial representation and the
bidirectional recurrent network. Neither uses the six catalogue features,
which catalogue entries do not have. Over five folds the trees score
{{SC_TREES}}, the network {{SC_NET}} and the mean of their probabilities
{{SC_MEAN}}. Each catalogue entry is scored with that mean.

Against the {{SV_NGAL}} galaxies and {{SV_NNOT}} non-galaxies of the inspected
sample, the mean separates the two with AUC {{SV_MEAN}}
({{SV_MEAN_LO}}--{{SV_MEAN_HI}}); the trees alone reach {{SV_TREES}} and the
network {{SV_NET}}. It also finds what the star flag misses: against only the
{{SV_NOSTAR_N}} non-galaxies the star flag passes, the AUC is {{SV_NOSTAR}}. The same pair trained on a different set
(catalogued galaxies against stars, and against Tractor fits fainter than the
selection window) scores {{SV_S2}}, below chance, so the training set matters more here than the architecture.

We flag entries that score below the weighted {{SF_LOWPCT}}th percentile of the
inspected galaxies' scores, so that the flag keeps {{SF_KEEP}}% of galaxies
([Fig. @fig-screen]). The threshold is cross-fitted: we split the sample at
random and set each half's threshold on the other half, so no object is
flagged by a threshold its own verdict helped set. By the sample weights
the flag marks {{SF_ENT}}% of entries, {{SF_GAL}}% of galaxies and
{{SF_NOT}}% of non-galaxies. Among the entries it passes the purity is {{SF_PASS}}%
({{SF_PASS_LO}}--{{SF_PASS_HI}}%), {{SF_GAIN}} percentage points
({{SF_GAIN_LO}}--{{SF_GAIN_HI}}) above the whole catalogue measured on the
same resamples. The whole improvement lies in the faint half, which rises from
{{SF_FAINT_ALL}}% to {{SF_FAINT_PASS}}%, while the bright half stays at
{{SF_BRIGHT_PASS}}%. A flagged entry is a galaxy {{SF_FLAGPUR}}% of the time
({{SF_FLAGPUR_LO}}--{{SF_FLAGPUR_HI}}%). The flag removes nothing, so the
selection function and the purity above describe the catalogue as released.

![The two-model flag on the inspected sample. (a) Scores of the
{{SV_NGAL}} galaxies and {{SV_NNOT}} non-galaxies, each class weighted to the
catalogue; the scores overlap, but the non-galaxies sit lower (AUC
{{SV_MEAN}}). Entries below the threshold are flagged; the darker band spans
the two cross-fitted thresholds. (b) Purity among the entries the flag passes,
against the share of entries it flags, with 95% bootstrap intervals. Each point
keeps a different fraction of the inspected galaxies, from all of them to 80%;
the large point is the flag used here, which keeps
{{SF_KEEP}}%.](figures/fig6_screen){#fig-screen}

# Comparison with DES and SMUDGes {#sec-compare}

The two published catalogues most similar to DEBBIE reached their purity in two
steps: an automated pipeline, then a visual check of every candidate it passed.
No DEBBIE entry was inspected individually, so the published figures for their
automated step are the ones to set beside DEBBIE's (@tbl-compare).

```{=latex}
\needspace{18\baselineskip}
```

| catalogue | imaging | selection | purity before the visual check | entries |
|:--------------|:---------------------|:----------------------------|:---------------|----------:|
| DES LSBG | DES Y3 | $r_{1/2} > 2.5''$, $\bar\mu_{\rm eff}(g) > 24.2$ | about 56% | 23,790 |
| SMUDGes V | Legacy Surveys DR9 | $\mu_{0,g} \ge 24$, $r_e \ge 5.3''$ | 92.4% | 7,070 |
| DEBBIE | Legacy Surveys DR10 | $r_{\rm eff} \ge 3''$, $24 \le \mu_{\rm eff}(g) \le 26.5$ | {{PF_A}}%, or {{SF_PASS}}% unflagged | {{N_COMMA}} |

: Without a visual check of each entry, DEBBIE's purity is close to the
SMUDGes pipeline's before its visual check and well above the DES pipeline's,
at {{CMP_X_DES}} and {{CMP_X_SM}} times their size. Surface brightnesses in mag arcsec$^{-2}$;
$r_{1/2}$ and $r_e$ are half-light radii and $\mu_{0,g}$ is the central
$g$-band surface brightness, each as its paper defines it. DES LSBG:
@tanoglidis2021cat, who estimate that 44% of
the objects their classifier passed are false positives, and their visual
inspection agreed. SMUDGes V: @zaritsky2023; 105 of 1,374 candidates were judged false
positives at visual review, and Papers II and III, quoted there, found 2.6%
and 2.8%, so 97.4% and 97.2% purity in those releases. DEBBIE: inspected stratified sample, with and without the two-model
flag (@sec-screen). {#tbl-compare}

The populations behind these numbers differ: DES keeps low-surface-brightness
galaxies and SMUDGes large diffuse ones, while most DEBBIE entries are ordinary galaxies at
$z \approx 0.3$ dimmed by distance (@sec-catalogue). Purity is also counted differently: theirs from candidates
an inspector rejected, ours from sampled entries with a galaxy at the
catalogued position. Both catalogues then removed what their inspectors
rejected, so their final purity should exceed DEBBIE's. What DEBBIE shows is
that an automated selection can reach the purity those pipelines had before
that step, at {{CMP_X_DES}} and {{CMP_X_SM}} times their size, with the purity
measured on an inspected sample.

# Summary {#sec-summary}

Light profiles in concentric annuli, classified with gradient-boosted trees,
match a published convolutional network on its own benchmark. With a recurrent
network they flag doubtful entries in DEBBIE, a catalogue too large to inspect entry by entry,
whose purity is measured on an inspected sample.

1. Gradient-boosted trees on annular light profiles reach AUC {{BM_AUC}} on the
   DeepShadows benchmark labels, against {{BM_SIX}} for six conventional catalogue
   features with the same classifier. Over five folds the paired improvement is
   ${{MM_GAIN}} \pm {{MM_GAIN_SD}}$, and averaging the trees with a recurrent
   network adds ${{MM_DUAL_D}}$.
2. DEBBIE holds {{N_COMMA}} galaxy candidates over about {{AREA_COMMA}}
   deg$^2$, nearly none inside the SDSS imaging footprint, with no prior
   identification as galaxies in HyperLEDA, SDSS DR12, GLADE+, the 2MASS XSC,
   2dFGRS, 6dFGS, SMUDGes, NED, SIMBAD or DESI DR1.
3. A galaxy lies at the catalogued position for {{PF_A}}% of entries
   ({{PF_A_LO}}--{{PF_A_HI}}%), from visual inspection of a stratified sample
   in two stages.
4. Boosted trees and a bidirectional recurrent network, retrained on the
   re-extracted benchmark, separate the inspected galaxies from non-galaxies
   with AUC {{SV_MEAN}}. Flagging the lowest-scoring {{SF_ENT}}% of entries
   raises purity among the rest to {{SF_PASS}}%.
5. Without inspecting each entry, that purity is close to the SMUDGes V
   pipeline's before its visual check (92.4%) and well above the DES search's
   at the same stage (about 56%), at {{CMP_X_DES}} and {{CMP_X_SM}} times
   the size of those catalogues.
6. A star flag trained on DESI spectra marks {{STAR_G_CLF}}% of Gaia stars it
   was not trained on, at the threshold that marks {{STAR_GLOSS}}% of
   spectroscopic galaxies.
7. Inside the selection window the photometric cuts retain 56--89% of known
   resolved galaxies, and the fragment filter removes {{FC_FRAG_PCT}}% of the
   candidates no catalogue lists.
8. The catalogue is substantially incomplete above
   $r_{\rm eff} \approx 15''$.
9. All redshifts are photometric. The median entry lies at $z = {{Z_MED}}$, so
   most entries are ordinary galaxies dimmed by distance, and
   {{N_DWARF_COMMA}} entries at $z < 0.05$ have the sizes and masses of dwarfs.

# Data availability

We release the catalogue as `DEBBIE.csv` ({{N_COMMA}} rows) with
`DEBBIE_lowb_extension.csv` ({{N_EXT_COMMA}} rows), version 1.4, each with an
ECSV copy and a SHA-256 checksum. The tables, the code and the source table
will be deposited at Zenodo, and the journal version carries both tables in
machine-readable form. @tbl-rows shows the first entries and @tbl-columns lists
the columns.
Designations take the form DEBBIE NNNNNN, a running number of up to six digits
written without leading zeros (DEBBIE 3 to DEBBIE 268380), and each entry also
carries a positional name of the form DEBBIE Jhhmmss.s$\pm$ddmmss. A number
is assigned once and never reused, so designations are stable across versions,
and the sequence has gaps where merged duplicates retired their numbers. The full selection can be
recomputed from the released 3.2 GB distilled source table (33.5 million
resolved sources, 31 columns), which reproduces the catalogue exactly.

```{=latex}
\needspace{14\baselineskip}
```

{{EXAMPLE_ROWS}}

: The first five entries of DEBBIE, by designation number. Positions in
degrees, $r_{\rm eff}$ in arcsec, $\mu_{\rm eff}(g)$ in mag arcsec$^{-2}$, $g$
and $g-r$ in mag. The full table, with positional names and every column of
@tbl-columns, is available in machine-readable form.
{#tbl-rows}

```{=latex}
\needspace{18\baselineskip}
```

| column | unit | contents |
|:-------------------------------|:-------------|:-----------------------------------------------------|
| `name`, `iau` | | designation (DEBBIE *N*) and coordinate-based name |
| `ra_deg`, `dec_deg` | deg | position from the DR10 sweeps |
| `position` | | the same position in sexagesimal form |
| `r_eff_arcsec` | arcsec | Tractor effective radius |
| `mu_eff_g` | mag arcsec$^{-2}$ | mean $g$ surface brightness within $r_{\rm eff}$ |
| `g_mag`, `g_r`, `r_z` | mag | $g$ magnitude and colours from Tractor fluxes, not corrected for Galactic extinction |
| `sersic` | | Tractor Sérsic index |
| `z_phot`, `z_source` | | photometric redshift and its source (`photo` for VII/292, `own` for ours) |
| `r_eff_kpc`, `M_g`, `log_mstar` | kpc, mag, dex | physical size, absolute magnitude and stellar mass, where a redshift exists; the mass is usable only at $z < 0.2$ |
| `pstar` | | Legacy Surveys star probability from VII/292 |
| `star_score`, `star_flag` | | star score and flag of @sec-stars |
| `prior_designations` | | designations from automated surveys, from NED |

: Columns of the released tables. {#tbl-columns}

# Limitations

The photometry is Tractor's [@lang2016], taken as published. Every redshift
is photometric, and {{OWN_PCT}}% come from our own estimator, which is trained
on photometric labels. That estimator's quoted scatter is
measured against the Legacy photo-$z$ and has not been tested against
spectroscopy, so those values should be used only for population statistics. Purity depends on
one inspector's verdicts for {{PUR_JUDGED}} objects (@sec-purity).
One radius, $r_{\rm eff} = 13.624''$, is recorded for {{N_PILE}} entries, which
suggests a cap on the radius in the Tractor fit. The
selection inherits Tractor's detection incompleteness, fails above
$r_{\rm eff} \approx 15''$, excludes $|b| < 30^\circ$ and is non-uniform on
the sky where prior surveys are deepest. Inside the SDSS imaging footprint it
is nearly empty, because SDSS had already catalogued most candidates there
(@sec-selfn).
